column3: This is an exact repetition of 21:7, including human messengers, revelation, and asking the people of remembrance.
Its unresponsive listeners contrast with the focus ayah's directive to seek knowledge, but do not clarify messenger humanity.
It directly explains why an angelic messenger would still have appeared as a human man.
It states that every earlier messenger received revelation, directly supporting the focus ayah's continuity claim.
The surah opening presents people as heedless and turning away, providing the immediate ignorance context for the command to ask.
It closely parallels revelation coming upon a man from the community to warn them.
It nearly repeats the focus claim that earlier messengers were men receiving revelation.
People hear a fresh reminder while playing, contrasting their response with the focus ayah's call to consult knowledge.
The men in the mosque and their purification do not clarify prophetic humanity, revelation, or inquiry.
The absence of prior books and warners for a community gives limited background to the sending of a warner.
The revealed Book described as a reminder gives context to the people of remembrance in the focus ayah.
Its faithful men are not about the status of messengers or the reception of revelation.
Earlier messengers having spouses and children directly reinforces their ordinary human condition.
Recognizing what is sent down from the Lord as truth provides a knowledge-and-revelation counterpart.
A man calls his people to follow the messengers, giving a limited response-side parallel.
The possibility of withholding the reminder from an excessive people gives a distant context for divine reminder.
The immediate objection that the messenger is merely human is the direct issue answered by 21:7.
Purification rules do not clarify the focus ayah's messengers, revelation, or inquiry.
The questioning of both recipients and messengers establishes their shared accountability under the sending of messengers.
The earth's mountains and paths do not add to the focus ayah.
Its use of men for humans and jinn is unrelated to prophetic humanity or revelation.
A messenger from among the people teaches the Book and what they did not know, closely extending the focus's instruction to seek knowledge.
Following guided messengers who seek no payment provides a practical response to their mission.
The rebuke about a short earthly stay and not knowing does not clarify the focus directive.
God's knowledge of every utterance is the immediate divine response within the same objection sequence.
The revealed reminder is sent to the messenger so that he may explain it to people, closely grounding recourse to informed guidance.
Mary and her son as a sign do not clarify the focus ayah's claim about male messengers.
The Friday call to God's remembrance is not a focused parallel to prophetic revelation or inquiry.
The challenge about the promised time does not clarify the focus ayah.
The men recognized by their marks in the Hereafter are unrelated to messenger identity.
The demand for a sign like earlier messengers received continues the same opponents' challenge to revelation.
The creation of male and female does not clarify the function of male human messengers.
Angelic reception of the righteous on the Last Day does not add to the focus claim.
The legal question and God's answer give only a formal parallel to asking for authoritative knowledge.
Its warning about worship and loss does not develop the focus ayah.
People of the Book who believe in revelations sent to both communities provide a secondary scriptural-knowledge parallel.
The preceding denial of faith by destroyed towns frames the opponents' skepticism before the focus ayah's answer.
The Quran as a possessor of remembrance gives a limited lexical context for the people of remembrance.
God fulfills His promise to the messengers and saves them, extending the historical messenger sequence stated in the focus.
It explicitly defines the message as revelation, directly clarifying the focus ayah's receiving of revelation.
The sudden inability to make a bequest or return home does not clarify the focus.
The deferred appointed term and forgiveness do not develop messenger humanity or inquiry.
The immediate next ayah states that the earlier messengers ate food and were not immortal, directly confirming their human condition.
The conduct of some people of the Book does not clarify the focus instruction to ask knowledgeable people.
Abraham's ironic command to ask idols contrasts asking competent knowers with asking those unable to speak.
Opponents reject the truth that came and expel the messenger, giving a secondary context for resistance to revelation.
The creation and ownership of livestock do not add to the focus ayah.
Its mention of men and women in human descent does not clarify male messengers or revelation.
The destruction and replacement of unjust towns does not explain the focus ayah.
The people of the Book demand a heavenly book and Musa receives clear authority, supplying a secondary revelation-and-questioning context.
The command to burn Abraham does not clarify messenger humanity, revelation, or inquiry.
The earth receiving divine inspiration is only a broad and non-prophetic use of revelation.
The preserved record of the dead does not clarify the focus ayah.
People questioning one another does not provide a substantive inquiry parallel.
The flight of a punished town does not clarify the focus claim.
The messenger's universal role as bearer of good news and warning extends his mission, though not his human nature.
The argument for God's oneness does not clarify messengers or asking knowledgeable people.
Nuh is sent to warn his people, giving a clear instance of the earlier messenger pattern.
The Quran is sent down in an intelligible language so that people may understand, providing a secondary knowledge-and-revelation parallel.
Nuh's commissioning as a clear warner supplies another earlier messenger instance.
The warning to return to worldly comforts does not clarify the focus ayah.
God reveals previously unknown reports to the messenger, directly showing revelation as the source of knowledge not otherwise possessed.
The sufficiency of the message for worshippers does not clarify messenger humanity or inquiry.
It explicitly says that all earlier messengers ate food and walked in markets, directly confirming their human condition.
The messenger clarifies what people of the Book concealed, providing a close explanatory role for revealed knowledge.
The command to ask earlier messengers about their message closely parallels inquiry into the established prophetic tradition.
The wrongdoers' confession does not clarify the focus ayah.
The messenger is sent as a bearer of good news and warning, extending the function of being sent.
God's knowledge of public and hidden speech does not add to the focus claim.
The repeated rejection of what warners bring gives a useful pattern of opposition to messengers.
The prohibition of intoxicants and gambling does not clarify the focus ayah.
It affirms an unchanging precedent for earlier messengers, supporting the focus ayah's historical continuity.
The destroyed people's repeated cry does not clarify messenger humanity or revelation.
It confirms many earlier messengers and their dependence on God's permission for signs.
Cosmic re-creation and the written scroll do not clarify the focus ayah.
It depicts a recurring rejection of warners through inherited custom, extending the focus context of skeptical opponents.
The rejection of invented animal taboos does not clarify the focus ayah.
The question of ownership of earth and its inhabitants is not a substantive parallel to consulting knowledgeable people.
Sulaiman and Dawud receive judgment and knowledge, but this does not specifically clarify human messengers receiving revelation.
God teaches people what they did not know, providing a limited knowledge-acquisition parallel.
The exclusive possession of intercession does not clarify the focus ayah.
Every messenger is sent in the language of his people to make the message clear, directly extending their human communicative role.
Sulayman's command over the wind does not clarify the focus ayah.
Those given knowledge state the truth at resurrection, but do not clarify prophetic inquiry.
Bringing and affirming truth gives only a general response to revealed truth.
It explicitly places earlier messengers and prophets within an ongoing revelatory process.
The queen's throne and dominion do not clarify the focus ayah.
A messenger is sent to be obeyed by God's permission, extending the purpose of sending him.
Iblis's threat to obstruct the straight path does not clarify the focus ayah.
Remembering depends on God's will, with only a distant lexical relation to the reminder.
The challenge concerning the revelation sent to God's servant affirms its divine source.
Hud's rescue from punishment does not clarify messenger humanity, revelation, or inquiry.
Verification in conflict does not clarify the focus's prophetic or knowledge claim.
The reference to revelation at Badr is incidental to rules for spoils and adds no focused value.
The destruction of prior plotters does not clarify the focus ayah.
The command concerning Salih's she-camel does not clarify the focus ayah.
The diversity of human striving does not clarify messengers, revelation, or inquiry.
The exception for God's devoted servants does not clarify the focus ayah.
God's sending of winds is unrelated to the sending of human messengers.
The bringing near of others at the sea does not clarify the focus ayah.
Ibrahim asks for a messenger from among the people to recite, teach the Book, and purify them.
God favors believers by sending among them a messenger who recites signs and teaches the Book and wisdom.
It explicitly places Muhammad's revelation in continuity with revelation to Nuh and the earlier prophets.
It names messengers whose accounts were told and untold, and specifically states that God spoke to Musa.
Messengers bear good news and warnings so humanity has no argument after their coming.
The messenger is commanded to convey what has been revealed to him from his Lord.
Messengers are sent as bearers of good news and warnings, extending the purpose of the sending named in the focus.
The messenger denies being an angel and says that he follows only what is revealed to him.
The Book given to Musa as light and guidance provides a concrete prior instance of prophetic revelation.
It rebuts objections to revelation by affirming that God knows best where to place His message.
It addresses humanity about messengers coming from among them to relate God's signs.
A messenger has come from among the people themselves, directly reinforcing a human and communal messenger.
It names the opponents' wonder that revelation came to a man from among them.
Every community has a messenger, directly extending the historical universality of the focus claim.
Messengers sent after Nuh brought clear proofs to their peoples, providing a sequence of prior missions.
Nuh's opponents object that he is only a human like them, closely matching the human-messenger dispute.
Nuh disclaims possession of divine treasures, the unseen, and angelic status, clarifying prophetic human limitation.
Messengers answer their peoples' doubt in God, providing a direct setting for contested prophetic address.
The messengers acknowledge that they are humans like their peoples, while God favors whom He wills.
God sends down and preserves the Reminder, clarifying the revealed reminder referenced in the focus.
God sends angels with the Spirit of His command to warn, directly explaining revelation's divine origin.
God raised a messenger in every community, strongly extending the focus's precedent of earlier messengers.
People's objection that God sent a human messenger is explicitly identified as what prevented their belief.
It explains that a messenger would be angelic only if angels lived securely on earth; human inhabitants receive human messengers.
The messenger is a human like his audience to whom revelation is given, making this a direct formulation of the focus claim.
Musa and Harun state that revelation has come to them, providing an explicit prophetic reception of revelation.
God chooses messengers from angels and from people, directly distinguishing the human messengers affirmed in the focus.
A people reject their messenger as merely a human like themselves, directly repeating the central objection answered by 21:7.
God sends to a community a messenger from among them, a direct human-messenger parallel.
Messengers are sent successively, establishing the continuity of prior prophetic missions.
Opponents challenge a messenger who eats food and walks in markets, directly paralleling the human condition explained by 21:7-8.
Salih's people object that he is only a human like them, extending the recurring rejection of human messengers.
Shuayb's people similarly call him only a human like themselves, another close human-messenger objection.
The sending of a warner to a people without a prior warner provides a boundary case for prophetic sending.
The messenger's duty is clear conveyance, extending the role of the one to whom revelation comes.
God sent messengers before Muhammad to their peoples, another direct statement of prophetic continuity.
The Quran is sent down to warn a people to whom no warner had come before, framing the significance of a messenger's arrival.
Muhammad is sent as witness, bearer of good news, and warner, expanding the mission of the sent messenger.
No community has passed without a warner, strongly supporting the focus ayah's historical scope.
It directly confirms that Muhammad is among the messengers.
A community's messengers are dismissed as human beings like their audience, a close parallel to the focus dispute.
The messengers affirm that God knows they were sent, reinforcing their commissioned status.
The messengers define their duty as clear delivery, extending the communication role of revelation.
Revelation to Muhammad and those before him is explicitly stated, directly confirming continuity of revelation.
Muhammad is a human like his audience to whom revelation is given, an especially close parallel to 21:7.
God reveals to Muhammad as He revealed to those before him, directly restating the focus's continuity.
It sets out the modes by which God communicates with a human, directly clarifying prophetic revelation.
It recalls how many prophets were sent among earlier peoples, supporting the focus ayah's historical argument.
Muhammad is not unprecedented among messengers and follows only what is revealed to him.
God sent messengers with clear proofs and sent down the Book and balance with them.
A messenger is raised among the unlettered people to recite signs and teach the Book and wisdom.
People reject clear proofs because they refuse to accept that a human being could guide them.
A messenger from God recites purified scriptures, giving a direct instance of revealed scripture delivered through a messenger.
